claim: The amnesic group was comprised of 16 participants with a mean age of 64.2 ± 4.81 years and included 3 females.
source: The amnesic group was comprised of 16 participants (mean and S.E.M. age: 64.2 ± 4.81 years, female = 3).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the demographic characteristics of the amnesic group.

claim: All participants in the amnesic group had chronic amnesia induced by leucine-rich glycine-inactivate-1 antibody-complex limbic encephalitis (LGI1-antibody-complex LE).
source: All participants in the amnesic group had chronic amnesia induced by a single-aetiology, leucine-rich glycine-inactivate-1 antibody-complex limbic encephalitis (LGI1-antibody-complex LE).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the etiology of amnesia in the study participants.

claim: The control group was comprised of 16 healthy age- and education-matched participants with a mean age of 62.3 ± 3.23 years and included 6 females.
source: Sixteen healthy age- and education-matched controls were recruited (62.3 ± 3.23 years, female = 2) to the control group.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the demographic characteristics of the control group. Note: There is a discrepancy in the abstract stating 'female = 6' versus the methods stating 'female = 2'.

claim: The amnesic group exhibited bilateral CA3 volume loss with a mean reduction of 29% compared to the control group.
source: Significant bilateral CA3 volume loss was seen in the amnesic group relative to the control group (F(1,28) = 14.52, p=0.001, Cohen's d = 1.39; mean reduction = –29%), whereas the differences in CA1, CA2, subiculum, and dentate gyrus volumes were not statistically significant at the Holm-Bonferroni alpha criterion corrected for multiple comparisons.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of hippocampal subfield volumes and Figure 2 shows the volume reduction in CA3.

claim: Whole-brain voxel-based morphometry revealed no evidence of significant gray matter volume loss outside of the hippocampus in the amnesic group relative to the control group.
source: The results revealed no suprathreshold clusters of gray matter volume loss in amnesic group participants relative to the control group.
evidence: The manuscript reports VBM analysis results and Figure 3 shows representative anatomical images.

claim: The amnesic group exhibited a loss of internal (episodic) detail for recent and remote memories, with the exception of the earliest remote memory (0-11 years).
source: Post hoc analyses revealed that the earliest remote memory (0–11 years) was intact (F(1,30) = 0.250, p=0.621), whereas there was temporally ungraded loss of internal detail across the remaining remote and recent memories (group: F(1,30) = 23.25, p<0.0001, η2p = 0.437; group x time: F(2.62,78.44) = 1.51, p=0.222, η2p = 0.048; time: F(2.62,78.44) = 0.604, p=0.592, η2p = 0.020), extending up to ~50 years prior to the CA3 damage (11–18 year interval for internal detail, F(1,30) = 6.43, p=0.017)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of Autobiographical Interview data and Figure 4 shows internal detail scores across time intervals.

claim: There was no significant between-group difference in the amount of external (semantic) detail remembered across the five time intervals.
source: There was no significant between-group difference in the amount of external (semantic) detail over the five intervals (F(1,30) = 1.24, p=0.275, η2p = 0.040)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of external detail scores and Figure 5 shows external detail scores across time intervals.

claim: The amnesic group exhibited increased average path length in nodes of the MTL subsystem of the default network, including left and right parahippocampal cortex, left retrosplenial cortex, left and right hippocampal formation, and ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
source: Compared to the control group, the amnesic group exhibited a loss of integration (increased average path length) in nodes of the MTL subsystem (Figure 7); namely, left and right parahippocampal cortex (MNI co-ordinates −28,–40,−12, β = −1.41, t = −3.51, p-FDR = 0.013 and MNI co-ordinates 28,–40,−12, β = −1.40, t = −3.53, p-FDR = 0.013, respectively), left retrosplenial cortex (MNI co-ordinates -14,-52,8, β = −0.75, t = −3.55, p-FDR = 0.013), left and right hippocampal formation (MNI co-ordinates −22,–20,−26, β = −0.93, t = −2.72, p-FDR = 0.033 and MNI co-ordinates 22,–20,26, β = −1.18, t = −2.99, p-FDR = 0.020, respectively), and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) (MNI co-ordinates 0, 26,–18, β = −1.52, t = −3.32, p-FDR = 0.020).
evidence: The manuscript reports graph theoretic analysis results and Figure 7 shows the affected nodes and their average path length differences.

claim: The amnesic group exhibited increased average path length in the left temporal pole of the dmPFC subsystem.
source: Increased average path length was also observed in the left temporal pole of the dmPFC subsystem (MNI co-ordinates −50,14,–40, β = −1.18, t = −3.34, p-FDR = 0.013).
evidence: The manuscript reports graph theoretic analysis results and Figure 7 shows the affected node.

claim: Local efficiency was significantly increased in three nodes: left posterior cingulate cortex, left parahippocampal cortex, and right retrosplenial cortex.
source: Local efficiency was significantly increased in three nodes: left posterior cingulate cortex (left PCC) (MNI co-ordinates −8,–56,26, β = 0.35, t = 3.49, p-FDR = 0.020), left parahippocampal cortex (left PHC) (MNI −28,–40,−12, β = 0.45, t = 3.25, p-FDR = 0.037) and right retrosplenial cortex (right Rsp) (MNI 14,–52,8, β = 0.36, t = 3.45, p-FDR = 0.020).
evidence: The manuscript reports graph theoretic analysis results and Figure 8 shows the affected nodes and their local efficiency differences.

claim: Differences in average path length from the control group mean in the left parahippocampal cortex, left and right hippocampal formation, left retrosplenial cortex, vmPFC, and left temporal pole significantly predicted the quantity of total internal (episodic) detail remembered by the amnesic group participants.
source: Differences in average path length from the mean of the control group in the left PHC (β = 1.05, t = 4.69, p=0.018), left hippocampal formation and right hippocampal formation (β = 1.81, t = 7.87, p=0.004 and β = −1.55, t = −8.66, p=0.003, respectively), left retrosplenial cortex (β = 26.61, t = 12.55, p=0.001), vmPFC (β = −26.31, t = −11.55, p=0.001), and the left temporal pole (β = −1.70, t = −10.26, p=0.002) significantly predicted the quantity of total internal (episodic) detail remembered by the amnesic group participants on the AI.
evidence: The manuscript reports robust multiple regression analysis results linking network topology to behavioral performance.

claim: CA3 volume and total internal detail were significantly correlated when collapsed across groups.
source: CA3 volume and total internal detail were significantly correlated (Kendall's τ (30) = 0.283, p=0.028, two-tailed; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), such that lower CA3 volumes were associated with remembering less internal detail on the AI, when these variables were collapsed across group.
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows the relationship between CA3 volume and internal detail.

claim: The amnesic group exhibited no significant deficits on standardized neuropsychological tests outside of memory, with the exception of delayed verbal recall.
source: Comprehensive assessment using standardized neuropsychological tests revealed that the scores for the amnesic group were comparable or significantly above normative data on composite measures of intelligence, attention, executive function, language, visuomotor skills, visuoconstruction skills, verbal memory, visual memory, and recognition memory (see 'Materials and methods' for individual subtest tests underlying the domain scores; Supplementary file 1a contains detailed results and N for each domain). Delayed verbal recall performance (which contributed to the verbal memory domain) was significantly different from normative data (N = 16, average z-score = −0.77, s.e.m. = 0.24, t(15) = –3.16, p=0.006), but above the threshold that typically indicates severe impairment (−1.67).
evidence: The manuscript reports neuropsychological assessment results and Figure 6 shows domain scores.

claim: LGI1-antibody-complex LE typically presents with amnesia and seizures and leads to non-reversible chronic atrophy that is confined to the hippocampus.
source: LGI1-antibody-complex LE typically presents with amnesia and seizures (Dalmau and Rosenfeld, 2014), and leads to non-reversible chronic atrophy that is confined to the hippocampus (Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2015b).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this characterization of LGI1-antibody-complex LE.

claim: In model organisms, LGI1 is predominantly expressed in CA3 and DG subfields.
source: In model organisms, LGI1 is predominantly expressed in CA3 and DG subfields (Herranz-Pérez et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on LGI1 expression in model organisms.

claim: Lesion and molecular imaging studies in rodents indicate that CA1 and CA3 enable the rapid storage and retrieval of recent (<1 month) contextual fear memories, whereas remote memories depend on CA1 but not CA3.
source: Lesion and molecular imaging studies in rodents indicate that CA1 and CA3 enable the rapid storage and retrieval of recent (<1 month) contextual fear memories, whereas remote memories depend on CA1 but not CA3 (Denny et al., 2014; Guzman et al., 2016; Kesner and Rolls, 2015; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Lisman, 1999; Lux et al., 2016; McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Rebola et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple rodent studies on the role of hippocampal subfields in memory.

claim: In humans, damage to CA1, associated with transient global amnesia, impairs recent and remote autobiographical episodic retrieval.
source: In humans, damage to CA1, associated with transient global amnesia (lasting, 8.3 ± 1.9 hr), impairs recent and remote autobiographical episodic retrieval (Bartsch et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the effects of CA1 damage in humans.

claim: In a recent study of a single case involving focal damage to the human dentate gyrus and a portion of CA3, secondary to hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury, deficits were found in recent and remote memories.
source: In a recent study of a single case involving focal damage to the human dentate gyrus and a portion of CA3, secondary to hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury, deficits were also found in recent and remote memories (Baker et al., 2016; Kwan et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites case studies on the effects of dentate gyrus and CA3 damage.

claim: Standard systems consolidation and computational-based theories predict that new hippocampal-dependent episodic memories become reorganized into a distributed neocortical network, such that remote memories are no longer dependent on the hippocampus.
source: In standard systems consolidation and computational-based theories of episodic memory, new hippocampal-dependent episodic memories become reorganized into a distributed neocortical network, such that remote memories are no longer dependent on the hippocampus (Bayley et al., 2005; Bontempi et al., 1999; Dudai and Morris, 2013; Kim and Fanselow, 1992; Kirwan et al., 2008; McClelland et al., 1995; Squire and Bayley, 2007; Takashima et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple theoretical and empirical studies supporting systems consolidation theory.

claim: According to multiple trace theory, the transformation hypothesis, contextual binding theory, and scene construction theory, episodic memory is hypothesized to be continuously dependent on the hippocampus for as long as the memory retains spatial detail and context-specific episodic content.
source: By contrast, according to multiple trace theory, the transformation hypothesis, contextual binding theory, and scene construction theory, episodic memory is hypothesized to be continuously dependent on the hippocampus for as long as the memory retains spatial detail and context-specific episodic content (Barry and Maguire, 2019; Maguire and Mullally, 2013; Moscovitch et al., 2016; Moscovitch et al., 2005; Winocur et al., 2010; Yonelinas et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple theoretical studies proposing continuous hippocampal involvement in episodic memory.

claim: The default network can be fractionated into a midline core, a MTL subsystem, and a dmPFC subsystem.
source: Applications of graph theoretic analyses and clustering analysis techniques to rs-fMRI have revealed that the DN can be fractionated into a midline core (posterior cingulate cortex and anterior medial prefrontal cortex [amPFC]), a MTL subsystem (ventral medial prefrontal cortex, posterior inferior parietal lobule, retrosplenial cortex, parahippocampal cortex, and hippocampal formation), and a dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) subsystem (dmPFC, temporo-parietal junction, lateral temporal cortex, and temporal pole) (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study that parcellated the default network into subsystems.

claim: The hippocampus acts as a major 'hub', linking different subnetworks that are involved in memory retrieval.
source: CA3 damage was also hypothesized to affect the functional connectivity of regions that have been implicated in autobiographical episodic memory, because the hippocampus acts as a major 'hub', linking different subnetworks that are involved in memory retrieval.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a rationale for examining functional connectivity, drawing on established knowledge about hippocampal function.

claim: Lesions involving hubs such as the hippocampus or other regions within the medial temporal lobe lead to disruption in the functional connectivity of non-local brain regions.
source: Lesions involving hubs such as the hippocampus or other regions within the medial temporal lobe (MTL) lead to disruption in the functional connectivity of non-local brain regions (Backus et al., 2016; Crossley et al., 2014; Mišić et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing that MTL lesions affect distant brain regions.

claim: The default network is associated with episodic retrieval.
source: Nodes and their pairwise ties or edges (the quantification of functional connectivity) were focused on the default network (DN) (Buckner et al., 2008; Buckner and DiNicola, 2019; Raichle et al., 2001), because the DN is associated with episodic retrieval (Raichle, 2015; Spreng and Grady, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies linking the default network to episodic retrieval.

claim: The default network overlaps with a network of regions associated with autobiographical memory, including parietal regions, medial prefrontal cortex, MTL, and lateral temporal cortex.
source: The DN also overlaps with a network of regions associated with autobiographical memory; namely, parietal regions such as posterior cingulate cortex/retrosplenial cortex, the medial prefrontal cortex, the MTL, and the lateral temporal cortex (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014; Buckner and Carroll, 2007; Cabeza and St Jacques, 2007; Greenberg et al., 2005b; Schacter et al., 2012; Spreng et al., 2009; Svoboda et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies linking the default network to autobiographical memory.

claim: All data were collected at the chronic phase of the LGI1-antibody-complex LE phenotype with a median time of 4 years between symptom onset and study examination.
source: All data were collected at the chronic phase of the LGI1-antibody-complex LE phenotype (time between symptoms onset and study examination: median = 4 years, range = 7), suggesting that the outcomes were unlikely to be mediated by short‐term compensatory processes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the timing of data collection relative to disease onset.

claim: The inter-rater correlation coefficient for scoring the Autobiographical Interview was 0.97.
source: The inter-rater correlation coefficient was calculated to be 0.97, across the internal and external detail scores, which is in line with the index study (Levine et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript reports the inter-rater reliability for the AI scoring.

claim: The amnesic group participants were comparable to the control group participants in their susceptibility to tangents during narrative construction.
source: Results from the analysis revealed that the amnesic group participants were comparable to the control group participants in their susceptibility to tangents during narrative construction (cumulative total tangents across five intervals: amnesic group = 0.20, control group = 0.63), which suggests that the deficits in the recollection of episodic detail were unlikely to reflect insufficiently supportive questioning during the adminstration of the AI.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of tangents during AI administration.

claim: The amnesic group used a similar number of words to describe episodes as the control group.
source: the use of a similar number of words to describe the episodes (amnesic group, total number of words = 106,047, mean number of words per interview = 6628, s.e.m. = 696; control group, total number of words = 97,654, mean number of words per interview = 6103, s.e.m = 500; t(15) = 0.59, p=0.56) suggests that the amnesic group autobiographical episodic memory deficit did not reflect a general impairment in verbal output (Barnett et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript reports word count analysis comparing the two groups.

claim: The amnesic group exhibited intact verbal fluency on the Graded Naming Test.
source: The absence of impairment in the retrieval of external (non-episodic, semantic) detail, intact verbal fluency on the Graded Naming Test (mean z-score = 0.75, s.e.m. = 0.28, t(15) = 2.71, p=0.016, two-tailed one-sample t-test)
evidence: The manuscript reports performance on the Graded Naming Test.

claim: The amnesic group exhibited preserved associative semantic memory on the Camel and Cactus Test.
source: Evidence for a null group difference in external detail aligns with the more general preservation of associative semantic memory (Camel and Cactus Test) (mean z-score = 0.20, s.e.m. = 0.30, t(14) = 0.67, p=0.514, two-tailed one-sample t-test) (Bozeat et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript reports performance on the Camel and Cactus Test.

claim: Delayed visual recall was intact in the amnesic group.
source: By contrast, delayed visual recall (comprised of Rey Delayed Recall) was intact (average z = −0.08, s.e.m. = 0.20, t(15) = 0.41, p=0.685).
evidence: The manuscript reports performance on delayed visual recall tests.

claim: There were no significant differences in functional connectivity between the amnesic group and control group for seed regions in the visual network and somatomotor network with the rest of the brain at a corrected p-FDR <0.05 threshold.
source: The additional analyses were consistent with these results, because there were no significant differences in functional connectivity between the amnesic group and the control group for the seed regions in the visual network and somatomotor network with the rest of the brain, when assessed at a corrected p-FDR <0.05 threshold.
evidence: The manuscript reports seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analysis results for control networks.

claim: Functional connectivity of the left and right hippocampal seed regions with the rest of the brain were not significantly different between the amnesic group and control group at a corrected p-FDR <0.05 threshold.
source: Unlike the effects found with MTL and larger hippocampal lesions (Hayes et al., 2012; Henson et al., 2016; Rudebeck et al., 2013), two sample independent t-tests revealed that functional connectivity of the left and right hippocampal seed-regions with the rest of the brain were not significantly different between the amnesic group and control group, when assessed at a corrected p-FDR <0.05 threshold.
evidence: The manuscript reports seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analysis results for hippocampal seeds.

claim: A significant group difference in functional connectivity was found between the right hippocampus seed ROI and the left PCC, but this difference did not survive Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
source: A significant group difference in functional connectivity was found between the right hippocampus seed ROI and the left PCC (t(27) = 1.75, p-FDR = 0.046). Hence, the only region that exhibited a between-group difference in functional connectivity with the hippocampus was the left PCC, but this difference did not survive Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
evidence: The manuscript reports ROI-to-ROI functional connectivity analysis results.

claim: None of the five control networks (somatomotor, visual, salience, ventral attention, and dorsal attention) exhibited altered topological properties in the amnesic group relative to the control group at p-FDR <0.05.
source: In the amnesic group, none of these networks exhibited altered topological properties in any of the graph theoretic measures relative to the control group at p-FDR <0.05 (see Supplementary files 1c–1g for results at p-FDR <0.05 and p-uncorrected <0.05 analysis thresholds).
evidence: The manuscript reports graph theoretic analysis results for control networks.

claim: Differences in local efficiency at the three affected nodes (left PHC, right retrosplenial cortex, and left PCC) did not significantly predict the quantity of internal (episodic) detail remembered by the amnesic group participants.
source: Differences in local efficiency at each of these three nodes from the mean of the control group did not significantly predict the quantity of internal (episodic) detail that was remembered by the amnesic group participants (Supplementary file 1r).
evidence: The manuscript reports robust multiple regression analysis results for local efficiency.

claim: Movement parameters were not significantly different between the amnesic and control groups.
source: Movement parameters were compared between the amnesic and control groups using two-tailed t-tests and revealed no significant between-group differences in mean framewise displacement, with amnesic and control participants exhibiting means of 0.23 mm (s.e.m. = 0.07 mm) and 0.26 mm (s.e.m. = 0.07 mm), respectively (t(27) = 0.570, p=0.573).
evidence: The manuscript reports motion analysis results from fMRI data.

claim: There were no significant correlations between altered topology and mean framewise displacement.
source: There were also no significant correlations between altered topology and mean framewise displacement (p-values >0.4).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis between motion and network topology.

claim: Dice similarities for hippocampal subfield segmentation were high, with a median of 0.79 for the amnesic group and 0.76 for the control group.
source: Dice similarities (amnesic group median = 0.79, control group median = 0.76) and intra-class correlation-coefficient-based metrics (amnesic group median = 0.98, control group median = 0.97) across lateralized subfield volumes demonstrated a high degree of reliability in the output of two full repetitions of the segmentation protocol in the entire dataset.
evidence: The manuscript reports reliability metrics for hippocampal subfield segmentation.

claim: Inter-rater Dice Similarity Indices for hippocampal subfield segmentation were reliable, with median values of 0.75 for the amnesic group and 0.74 for the control group.
source: Inter-rater Dice Similarity Indices (DSIs) of two independent raters for the amnesic group and control group were also reliable (median amnesic group and control group DSIs across all subfields: 0.75 and 0.74, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports inter-rater reliability for hippocampal subfield segmentation.

claim: Left and right CA3 exhibited comparable volume loss of 29% in the amnesic group when contrasted against the control group.
source: Notably, left (mean volume loss = -29%, SEM = 0.04) and right (mean volume loss = -29%, SEM = 0.03) CA3 exhibited comparable volume loss in the amnesic group (N = 15) when contrasted against the corresponding control mean CA3 volumes (N = 15).
evidence: The manuscript reports lateralized CA3 volume loss.

claim: A relative reduction in CA3 volumes was observed in all amnesic group participants.
source: A relative reduction in CA3 volumes to their matched control was observed in all amnesic group participants.
evidence: The manuscript states that all amnesic participants showed CA3 volume reduction.

claim: CA1 volume loss was not significant when the alpha criterion was corrected for multiple comparisons.
source: Also in line with our prior study of 18 amnesic participants with LGI1-antibody-complex LE, CA1 volume loss was not significant when the alpha criterion was corrected for multiple comparisons (mean volume loss = -16%, F(1,28) = 5.25, p-uncorrected = 0.019, Cohen's d = 0.91).
evidence: The manuscript reports CA1 volume analysis results.

claim: The observed selectivity of CA3 volume loss is consistent with the anatomical localization of enrichment of LGI1 gene transcripts in CA3 of the adult human brain.
source: The observed selectivity of CA3 volume loss is consistent with the anatomical localization of enrichment of LGI1 gene transcripts in CA3 of the adult human brain (Hawrylycz et al., 2012), the expression of LGI1 gene transcripts in mouse CA3 (Herranz-Pérez et al., 2010), and evidence of greater neuronal loss in CA3 compared to CA1 following seizures in homozygous LGI1 knockout mice (Chabrol et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on LGI1 expression and relates them to the observed CA3 volume loss.

claim: CA3 exhibits particular vulnerability to excitotoxic lesions associated with seizures compared to CA1.
source: When compared to CA1, CA3 exhibits particular vulnerability to excitotoxic lesions associated with seizures, given that IgG-containing LGI1 antibodies induce population epileptiform discharges either in CA3 pyramidal neurons in vitro (Lalic et al., 2011), or from complement-mediated fixation of bound antibodies (Bien et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the vulnerability of CA3 to seizure-related damage.

claim: The chronic phase of LGI1-antibody-complex LE represents a compelling lesion model for studying the causal role of human CA3 in the hippocampal network.
source: Evidence of selective anatomical damage associated with LGI1 pathogenesis suggests that the chronic phase of the disease represents a compelling lesion model for studying the causal role of human CA3 in the hippocampal network.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference about the utility of this patient population for studying CA3 function.

claim: The duration of CA3 involvement in autobiographical episodic retrieval is at variance with evidence from model organisms that suggests remote memories depend on CA1 but not CA3.
source: The duration of CA3 involvement in autobiographical episodic retrieval is at variance with the evidence from model organisms that suggests that remote memories depend on CA1 but not CA3 (Denny et al., 2014; Guzman et al., 2016; Kesner and Rolls, 2015; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Lisman, 1999; Lux et al., 2016; McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Rebola et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript compares the current findings to prior animal studies.

claim: The loss of episodic detail for recent and remote memories is consistent with neurobiological accounts that predict damage to the human hippocampus affects retrieval for as long as the memory retains vivid, episodic detail.
source: The loss of episodic detail for recent and remote memories (i.e., for all but the earliest remote memory) is consistent with neurobiological accounts that predict damage to the human hippocampus affects retrieval for as long as the memory retains vivid, episodic detail (Barry and Maguire, 2019; Eichenbaum et al., 2007; Hassabis and Maguire, 2007; Moscovitch et al., 2016; Nadel and Moscovitch, 1997; Winocur et al., 2007; Yonelinas et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript relates the findings to theoretical accounts of hippocampal function in memory.

claim: The preservation of the earliest remote memories is consistent with the contention that these memories are remembered more frequently, re-encoded, and can be supported by neocortical representations.
source: The preservation of the earliest remote memories is consistent with the contention that these memories are remembered more frequently, re-encoded, and can be supported by neocortical representations (Sekeres et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study and draws an inference about the nature of early remote memories.

claim: Impaired recall of detailed episodic memories in the amnesic group could reflect a diminution in the ability to discriminate between individual mnemonic patterns and/or to track the precision of episodic retrieval for specific events with partial cueing.
source: Impaired recall of detailed episodic memories in the amnesic group could thus, in part, reflect a diminution in the ability of these participants to discriminate between individual mnemonic patterns and/or to track the precision of episodic retrieval for specific events with partial cueing (Chadwick et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the computational mechanisms underlying the observed memory deficits.

claim: The effects of the CA3 damage on default network topology may help to explain the gap between the small bilateral subfield damage and persistent episodic memory loss.
source: The effects of the CA3 damage on DN topology may help to explain the notional gap between the small, by volume, bilateral subfield damage observed here and persistent episodic memory loss.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference about the relationship between anatomical damage and functional connectivity changes.

claim: The reduction in functional integration in the amnesic group aligns with the impact of damage to hub regions having a disproportionate effect on global efficiency.
source: The reduction in functional integration — that is, the capacity to transmit information with less attenuation — in the amnesic group aligns with the impact of damage to hub regions, such as the hippocampus, having a disproportionate effect on global efficiency (Hwang et al., 2013 Albert et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the effects of hub damage and relates them to the observed findings.

claim: The loss of integration in parahippocampal cortices is likely to have interfered with the operations necessary for remembering episodic detail.
source: Parahippocampal cortices support context reinstatement (Diana et al., 2013) and remote memory (Lux et al., 2016), thus the loss of integration in parahippocampal cortices is likely to have interfered with the operations necessary for remembering episodic detail.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on parahippocampal function and draws an inference about the impact of altered connectivity.

claim: Integration between the affected regions and other parts of the core autobiographical network is particularly important for successful episodic retrieval.
source: Integration between the affected regions and other parts of the core autobiographical network is particularly important for successful episodic retrieval (Westphal et al., 2017), and is likely to impact on the capacity of hippocampal-neocortical ensembles to support the reconstruction and elaboration that underscores autobiographical episodic retrieval (Barry and Maguire, 2019; Greenberg et al., 2005a; Piolino et al., 2009; St-Laurent et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on network integration and episodic retrieval.

claim: Functional coupling between the hippocampus and retrosplenial cortex has been implicated in the initial reconstruction of the episodic context and detail as a memory is selected and accessed.
source: For example, functional coupling between the hippocampus and retrosplenial cortex has been implicated in the initial reconstruction of the episodic context and detail as a memory is selected and accessed (Inman et al., 2018), and supports the consolidation of events (Bird et al., 2015; Staresina et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on hippocampal-retrosplenial interactions in memory.

claim: Increases in local efficiency may alter connectivity with immediately surrounding regions that support the regulation of learning, consolidation, and retrieval, and could reflect adaptive functional reorganization.
source: Increases in local efficiency may alter connectivity with immediately surrounding regions that support the regulation of learning, consolidation, and retrieval, and could reflect adaptive functional reorganization, possibly involving the reassignment of nodal roles.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the functional significance of increased local efficiency.

claim: In model organisms, the inhibition of rodent CA1 can lead to selective compensatory changes in anterior cingulate cortex activity, which are associated with remote contextual memory.
source: In model organisms, the inhibition of rodent CA1 can lead to selective compensatory changes in anterior cingulate cortex activity, which are associated with remote contextual memory (Goshen et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on compensatory changes following CA1 inhibition in rodents.

claim: Increases in local efficiency of between 85% and 270% have been observed in structural connectivity studies of left temporal lobe epilepsy, attributed to a compensatory mechanism that maintains connectivity despite the loss of connections in hub regions.
source: Increases in local efficiency of between 85% and 270% have been observed in structural connectivity studies of left temporal lobe epilepsy, and attributed to a compensatory (perhaps maladaptive) mechanism that maintains connectivity despite the loss of connections in hub regions (DeSalvo et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on local efficiency changes in epilepsy.

claim: The effects of hippocampal and MTL damage on resting-state networks have variable scalar extents across mixed aetiologies.
source: The effects of hippocampal and MTL damage, which are observed across mixed aetiologies, on RSNs have variable scalar extents (Hayes et al., 2012; Heine et al., 2018; Henson et al., 2016; Rudebeck et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing variability in the effects of MTL damage on brain networks.

claim: The observed scalar extent of altered network topology aligns with evidence that simulated lesions involving hub regions can lead to non-extensive effects on topological organization.
source: Also in line with the observed scalar extent of altered network topology is evidence that simulated lesions involving hub regions can lead to non-extensive effects on topological organization, whereas damage to regions that connect different network modules (connectors) can result in widespread effects that affect whole-brain network organization (Gratton et al., 2012; He et al., 2009; Honey and Sporns, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the effects of hub versus connector lesions and relates them to the current findings.

claim: Larger-scale effects on graph theoretic measures of functional connectivity have been reported following more extensive damage.
source: Larger-scale effects on graph theoretic measures of functional connectivity have, however, been reported following more extensive damage (Henson et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing more widespread effects with extensive damage.

claim: Alterations in connectivity between the hippocampus and the posterior cingulate cortex are likely to disrupt autobiographical memory.
source: Alterations in connectivity between the hippocampus and the posterior cingulate cortex are likely to disrupt autobiographical memory, because functional connectivity between the hippocampus and the posterior cingulate cortex has been implicated in episodic autobiographical remembering (Sheldon et al., 2016; Sheldon and Levine, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on hippocampal-PCC connectivity and draws an inference about the impact of altered connectivity.

claim: More extensive damage to the hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and temporal pole can lead to significant differences in functional connectivity that are limited to the default network.
source: More extensive damage to the hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and temporal pole can lead to significant differences in functional connectivity that are limited to the DN (Hayes et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the effects of more extensive MTL damage.

claim: Other studies have observed dysfunction in multiple large-scale brain networks following hippocampal damage.
source: Other studies, however, have observed dysfunction in multiple large-scale brain networks following hippocampal damage, such that functional connectivity was decreased in the salience network and increased in the dorsal and ventral DN, sensorimotor network, and higher visual networks relative to that in control participants (Heine et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing widespread network effects following hippocampal damage.

claim: White matter connectivity appears to be unaffected by LGI1-antibody-complex LE.
source: It is important to note, however, that white matter connectivity appears to be unaffected by LGI1-antibody-complex LE (Finke et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on white matter integrity in LGI1-antibody-complex LE.

claim: CA3 along with CA2 and the DG are input structures typically associated with encoding, whereas CA1 is an output structure implicated in the retrieval of events within their temporal context.
source: CA3 along with CA2 and the DG are input structures, typically associated with encoding, whereas CA1 is an output structure, implicated in the retrieval of events within their temporal context (Preston et al., 2010; Suthana et al., 2011; Zeineh et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the functional roles of hippocampal subfields.

claim: In healthy adult participants, CA3 volume correlates with the efficacy with which newly formed memories are differentiated.
source: In healthy adult participants, there has been a failure to find an association between CA1 volume and episodic retrieval (Mueller et al., 2011), whereas CA3 volume correlates with the efficacy with which newly formed memories are differentiated (Chadwick et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the relationship between hippocampal subfield volumes and memory function.

claim: fMRI studies based on laboratory-learned materials suggest that time and space context are represented across multiple human hippocampal subfields.
source: fMRI studies based on laboratory-learned materials suggest that time and space context are represented across multiple human hippocampal subfields (Copara et al., 2014), with differentiation between spatial and temporal context mediated by distinct neural network patterns (i.e., multiplexed) rather than by individual structures (Kyle et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites fMRI studies on context representation in hippocampal subfields.

claim: Residual bilateral MTL volume following brain injury correlates with remote autobiographical memory.
source: Volumetric analyses that collapse across larger subregions have found that, for example, residual bilateral MTL volume following brain injury correlates with remote autobiographical memory (Gilboa et al., 2005)
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on MTL volume and remote memory.

claim: In participants who underwent temporal lobe resection for epilepsy, right parahippocampal cortical volumes correlated with the capacity to remember remote episodes and bilateral MTL regions predicted memory for recent episodes.
source: whereas in a study on participants who underwent temporal lobe resection for epilepsy, right parahippocampal cortical volumes correlated with that capacity to remember remote episodes and bilateral MTL regions predicted memory for recent episodes (Noulhiane et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on MTL volumes and episodic memory in epilepsy patients.

claim: Human CA3 may be a default activator of remote episodic memories that participates in their maintenance throughout recall.
source: Human CA3 may be a default activator of remote episodic memories that participates in their maintenance throughout recall (Goshen et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the role of CA3 in remote memory, citing a rodent study.

claim: CA3 damage is likely to impair normal engagement with neocortical episodic memory traces, because CA3 enables signals arising from different brain regions to be associated together.
source: CA3 damage is likely to impair normal engagement with neocortical episodic memory traces, because CA3 enables signals arising from different brain regions to be associated together (Kesner and Rolls, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on CA3 function and draws an inference about the impact of CA3 damage.

claim: The current results extend experimental evidence on the neural basis of episodic memory to highlight the important role of integration in the MTL subsystem.
source: The current results also extend experimental evidence on the neural basis of episodic memory to highlight the important role of integration in the MTL subsystem (Geib et al., 2017; Westphal et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on MTL subsystem integration and relates them to the current findings.

claim: Different multiscale brain circuits are recruited during recent and remote memory.
source: Future work will need to hone in on how intrinsic hippocampal subfield-based computations contribute to autobiographical memory and how subfield involvement in episodic memory changes with use, especially because different multiscale brain circuits are recruited during recent and remote memory (Barry and Maguire, 2019; Dudai and Morris, 2013; Nader and Hardt, 2009; Tronson and Taylor, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the dynamic nature of memory circuits over time.

claim: The known timing, discrete onset, and monophasic nature of autoimmune encephalitis suggest that hippocampal function was intact in these participants during the encoding of memories before the disease onset.
source: Unlike studies of amnesia involving participants with chronic conditions such as epilepsy that are associated with seizures and hippocampal sclerosis (Kapur and Prevett, 2003), the known timing, discrete onset, and monophasic nature of autoimmune encephalitis suggest that hippocampal function was intact in these participants during the encoding of memories before the disease onset.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference about the encoding of pre-morbid memories based on the disease characteristics.

claim: Impaired retrograde memory probably reflects disruption of CA3-mediated retrieval mechanisms rather than anterograde difficulties with encoding and consolidation.
source: Hence, impaired retrograde memory probably reflects disruption of CA3-mediated retrieval mechanisms rather than anterograde difficulties with encoding and consolidation.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference about the nature of the memory deficit based on the disease characteristics.

claim: All participants in the amnesic group were seizure-free at the time of testing.
source: All participants were seizure-free at the time of testing.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the seizure status of participants at testing.

claim: All participants in the amnesic group were considered clinically stable by their consultant neurologist and were discharged and not undergoing treatment.
source: All of the amnesic group participants were considered clinically stable by their consultant neurologist (median = 4 years post-onset, range = 7), and were thus discharged and not undergoing treatment.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the clinical status of amnesic participants.

claim: All participants in the amnesic group were otherwise self-reported as healthy, with no evidence of secondary gain or active psychopathology.
source: All participants with amnesia were otherwise self-reported as healthy, with no evidence of secondary gain or active psychopathology.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the health status of amnesic participants.

claim: All participants in the control group had no history of cognitive, psychiatric, or neurological illness, and were not taking psychoactive medications.
source: These participants had no history of cognitive, psychiatric, or neurological illness, and were not taking psychoactive medications.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the health status of control participants.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, with the exception of one participant in the amnesic group who had reduced visual fields secondary to age-related macular degeneration.
source: With the exception of one participant in the amnesic group who had reduced visual fields, secondary to age-related macular degeneration, all participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the visual status of participants.

claim: All participants were fluent, native English speakers.
source: All participants were fluent, native English speakers.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the language status of participants.

claim: No significant differences were found between the groups in terms of age or years-of-education.
source: No significant differences were found between the groups in terms of age or years-of-education.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that groups were matched on age and education.

claim: All acquired events on the Autobiographical Interview were verified against a collateral for confabulation, and no evidence of confabulation was found.
source: In line with prior studies of autobiographical memory (Tranel and Jones, 2006), each narrative was verified, where possible, against a collateral – a spouse, family member, or friend – for confabulation (differences in personal reflections and thoughts notwithstanding). No evidence of confabulation was found.
evidence: The manuscript reports verification of autobiographical memories.

claim: Fifteen of the participants in the amnesic group were LGI1-antibody positive and one participant was LGI1 and CASPR2 negative but VGKC-complex antibody positive.
source: Fifteen of the participants were LGI1-antibody positive and one participant was LG1I and CASPR2 negative but VGKC-complex antibody positive.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the antibody status of participants.

claim: Auto-antibodies to LGI1 and CASPR2 proteins are preferentially expressed in CA3 and CA1.
source: Auto-antibodies to the two principal antigenic components of the voltage-gated potassium channel (VGKC)-complex—LGI1 and CASPR2 proteins—are preferentially expressed in CA3 and CA1 (Irani et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the expression of LGI1 and CASPR2 antibodies.

claim: The anatomical localization of enrichment of LGI1 gene transcripts in CA3 of the adult human brain has been documented.
source: The observed selectivity of CA3 volume loss is consistent with the anatomical localization of enrichment of LGI1 gene transcripts in CA3 of the adult human brain (Hawrylycz et al., 2012)
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on LGI1 gene expression in the human brain.

claim: Evidence of greater neuronal loss in CA3 compared to CA1 following seizures in homozygous LGI1 knockout mice has been reported.
source: and evidence of greater neuronal loss in CA3 compared to CA1 following seizures in homozygous LGI1 knockout mice (Chabrol et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on neuronal loss in LGI1 knockout mice.

claim: IgG-containing LGI1 antibodies induce population epileptiform discharges in CA3 pyramidal neurons in vitro.
source: given that IgG-containing LGI1 antibodies induce population epileptiform discharges either in CA3 pyramidal neurons in vitro (Lalic et al., 2011)
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the effects of LGI1 antibodies on CA3 neurons.

claim: Complement-mediated fixation of bound antibodies can cause neuronal loss in CA3.
source: or from complement-mediated fixation of bound antibodies (Bien et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on complement-mediated damage from antibodies.

claim: No other lesions were detected in any of the amnesic group participants.
source: No other lesions were detected in any of the amnesic group participants.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of other lesions.

claim: Hippocampal area CA3 supports computations that distinguish between specific experiences (pattern separation) or that code relationships across items to increase overlap (pattern completion).
source: Hippocampal area CA3 supports computations that distinguish between specific experiences (pattern separation) or that code relationships across items to increase overlap (pattern completion) (Aly and Turk-Browne, 2016; Guzman et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2004; McClelland et al., 1995; Norman and O'Reilly, 2003; Treves and Rolls, 1994; Yassa and Stark, 2011), depending on the degree of similarity or dissimilarity between contexts or learning materials (Guzowski et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies on CA3 computational functions.

claim: The observed deficit in episodic memory was specific, because the loss of internal detail was expressed under conditions where personal semantic detail was intact relative to that in the control group.
source: Notably, the observed deficit was specific, because the loss of internal (episodic) detail was expressed under conditions where personal semantic (external) detail was intact relative to that in the control group, which aligns with the effects of bilateral and unilateral temporal lobe resection (Noulhiane et al., 2007; Viskontas et al., 2000) and other results reported in studies of hippocampal damage (Taylor et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the specificity of episodic memory deficits following hippocampal damage.

claim: The impact of deficits in pattern separation and pattern completion computations on remote and recent episodic detail retrieval may not be equivalent, because remote memories are likely to have undergone more extensive reconsolidation and reconstruction.
source: It is also worth noting that the impact of deficits in these computations on remote and recent episodic detail retrieval may not be equivalent, because remote memories are likely to have undergone more extensive reconsolidation and reconstruction (Barry and Maguire, 2019; Dudai and Morris, 2013; Nader and Hardt, 2009; Tronson and Taylor, 2007; Wang and Morris, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on memory reconsolidation and draws an inference about differential effects on recent versus remote memories.

claim: Hippocampal and CA3/DG activity measured using fMRI have each been associated with the retrieval of remote autobiographical episodic detail across a wide range of intervals.
source: Remote memories remain hippocampal-dependent in mice when detailed context fear memories are assessed (Wiltgen et al., 2010), whereas in humans, hippocampal and CA3/DG activity measured using fMRI have each been associated with the retrieval of remote autobiographical episodic detail across a wide range of intervals (mean range = −2.5 days to −32.3 years) (Bonnici et al., 2012; Gilboa et al., 2004; Rekkas and Constable, 2005; Söderlund et al., 2012; Steinvorth et al., 2006; Viard et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple fMRI studies on hippocampal involvement in remote memory retrieval.

claim: Early memories have been described as gist-like.
source: Early memories have been described as gist-like (Hardt et al., 2013; Richards and Frankland, 2017; Sadeh et al., 2014), and are arguably qualitatively different from other remote memories along several dimensions (Barclay and Wellman, 1986; Cermak, 1984; Sekeres et al., 2018; Winocur and Moscovitch, 2011), lose contextual specificity over time, and can be supported by extra-hippocampal regions such as the medial prefrontal cortex (Clewett et al., 2019; Wiltgen et al., 2010; Winocur et al., 2010; Winocur et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies on the nature of early remote memories.

claim: The earliest, intact remote memory may not be hippocampal (CA3)-dependent.
source: By inference, the earliest, intact remote memory may not be hippocampal (CA3)-dependent.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference about the hippocampal dependence of the earliest remote memories.

claim: The earliest remote memories were not detectably schematized to a state that rendered them qualitatively different from the more recent (remote) memories, at least when assessed by examining the ratio between external and internal detail.
source: Hence, the earliest remote memories were not detectably schematized to a state that rendered them qualitatively different from the more recent (remote) memories, at least when assessed by examining the ratio between external and internal detail.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of the ratio of external to internal detail for the earliest remote memories.

claim: Retrograde amnesia was temporally ungraded across recent and remote memories and spanned up to ~50 years prior to CA3 damage.
source: Hence, this post hoc analysis revealed that the loss of internal detail in the amnesic group did not change across these recent and remote memories (i.e., it was temporally ungraded/a flat gradient), and spanned up to ~50 years prior to CA3 damage (11–18 year interval for internal detail, F(1,30) = 6.43, p=0.017), when the loss was assessed without the earliest, intact remote memory.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing temporally ungraded retrograde amnesia.

claim: The loss of internal detail was time-sensitive: retrograde amnesia was temporally ungraded across recent and remote memories and spanned up to ~50 years prior to CA3 damage, whereas the earliest remote memory was intact.
source: Together, these post hoc analyses revealed that the loss of internal detail was time-sensitive: retrograde amnesia was temporally ungraded across recent and remote memories and spanned up to ~50 years prior to CA3 damage, whereas the earliest remote memory was intact.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the pattern of memory loss across time intervals.

claim: The deficits in recent and remote memory are unlikely to be secondary to impairments in cognitive faculties that are necessary for autobiographical retrieval, such as attention, language, and executive function.
source: Hence, the deficits in recent and remote memory are unlikely to be secondary to impairments in cognitive faculties that are necessary for autobiographical retrieval, such as attention, language, and executive function.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference about the specificity of the memory deficit based on intact performance on other cognitive domains.

claim: Delayed recall is sensitive to hippocampal damage.
source: In terms of standardized tests of memory, there were no significant deficits evident on the composite indices outside of delayed verbal recall (comprised of Logical Memory II, Logical Memory II themes and Word Lists II [WMS-III] and the People Recall Test) (n = 16, average z-score = −0.77, s.e.m. = 0.24, t(15) = –3.16, p=0.006), which is in line with evidence that delayed recall is sensitive to hippocampal damage (Aggleton and Shaw, 1996; Mayes et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the sensitivity of delayed recall to hippocampal damage.

claim: Prior studies have shown that the chronic phase of the LGI1-antibody-complex LE phenotype is associated with persistent memory deficits, particularly in episodic verbal memory.
source: Prior studies have shown that the chronic phase of the LGI1-antibody-complex LE phenotype is associated with persistent memory deficits (Bettcher et al., 2014; Butler et al., 2014; Malter et al., 2014), particularly in episodic verbal memory (Finke et al., 2017; McCormick et al., 2016; McCormick et al., 2017; McCormick et al., 2018b; Miller et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies on memory deficits in LGI1-antibody-complex LE.

claim: The evidence of intact recognition memory suggests that the deficit in autobiographical episodic detail in the amnesic group was not due to a general inability to remember.
source: The evidence of intact recognition memory suggests that the deficit in autobiographical episodic detail in the amnesic group was not due to a general inability to remember (Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference about the specificity of the memory deficit based on intact recognition memory.

claim: The specificity of impairment accompanying CA3 damage is broadly consistent with the hypothesis that damage to hub regions, which underpin subnetworks relevant for specific cognitive functions, can generate specific cognitive deficits.
source: The specificity of impairment accompanying CA3 damage is broadly consistent with the hypothesis that damage to hub regions, which underpin subnetworks relevant for specific cognitive functions, can generate specific cognitive deficits (Gratton et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on hub damage and draws an inference about the specificity of deficits.

claim: Broader cognitive deficits are more likely to occur when damage involves connector regions (which co-ordinate between multiple subnetworks).
source: It is conceivable that broader cognitive deficits are more likely to occur when damage involves connector regions (which co-ordinate between multiple subnetworks) (Gratton et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study and speculates about the relationship between lesion location and cognitive deficits.

claim: Focal damage limited to human CA1 in a group of 16 participants, secondary to acute transient global amnesia, was associated with deficits on verbal and visuoconstructive memory tests, whereas naming and conceptual knowledge, general intellectual abilities, and visual attention were intact.
source: More focal damage limited to human CA1 in a group of 16 participants, secondary to acute transient global amnesia (lasting 8.3 ± 1.9 hr), was associated with deficits on verbal and visuoconstructive memory tests, whereas naming and conceptual knowledge, general intellectual abilities, and visual attention were intact (Bartsch et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the cognitive profile following CA1 damage.

claim: Anatomical damage associated with the chronic phase of the LGI1-antibody-complex LE phenotype did not lead to gray matter volume loss outside of the hippocampus.
source: In prior 3.0-Tesla and 7.0-Tesla MRI based studies, we showed that anatomical damage associated with the chronic phase of the LGI1-antibody-complex LE phenotype did not lead to gray matter volume loss outside of the hippocampus (McCormick et al., 2016; McCormick et al., 2017; McCormick et al., 2018b; Miller et al., 2017) (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies and refers to Figure 3 showing the absence of extra-hippocampal volume loss.

claim: Evidence of focal hippocampal damage aligns with the results from other laboratories on the anatomical sequalae of LGI1-antibody-complex LE.
source: Such evidence of focal hippocampal damage aligns with the results from other laboratories on the anatomical sequalae of LGI1-antibody-complex LE (Finke et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2015b; Wagner et al., 2015a).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies from other laboratories supporting focal hippocampal damage in LGI1-antibody-complex LE.

claim: CA3 is not considered a main output structure, because it receives sparse, orthogonalized input via the mossy fibers from the DG, but nonetheless has outputs via the fimbria that can bypass CA1.
source: CA3 is not considered a main output structure, because it receives sparse, orthogonalized input via the mossy fibers from the DG, but nonetheless has outputs via the fimbria that can bypass CA1 (van Strien et al., 2009; Witter and Amaral, 2004), which suggests that the effects of CA3 damage are likely to involve changes in the functional connectivity of non-local brain regions.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on CA3 connectivity and draws an inference about the effects of CA3 damage.

claim: Evidence from the inhibition of rodent CA1 indicates that selective compensatory changes can occur in anterior cingulate cortex activity.
source: Evidence from the inhibition of rodent CA1 indicates that selective compensatory changes can occur in anterior cingulate cortex activity (Goshen et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on compensatory changes following CA1 inhibition.

claim: The effects of CA3 damage are likely to involve changes in the functional connectivity of non-local brain regions.
source: which suggests that the effects of CA3 damage are likely to involve changes in the functional connectivity of non-local brain regions.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference about the effects of CA3 damage based on its anatomical connectivity.

claim: Functional connectivity can reflect signaling that unfolds within the underlying structural network.
source: More generally, because functional connectivity can reflect signaling that unfolds within the underlying structural network (Betzel et al., 2013; Goñi et al., 2014), future studies will need to examine anatomical pathways.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the relationship between functional and structural connectivity.

claim: fMRI and neuropsychological studies indicate that the retrieval of autobiographical and experimentally determined encoded memories are dissociable.
source: fMRI and neuropsychological studies indicate that the retrieval of autobiographical and experimentally determined encoded memories are dissociable (McDermott et al., 2009; Palombo et al., 2015; Patihis et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the dissociation between autobiographical and laboratory-based memory.

claim: The behavioral results from the AI and mild impairment on standardized measures of recall are compatible with the hypothesis that, under some conditions, the retrieval of autobiographical event knowledge is qualitatively different from other forms of episodic retrieval.
source: The behavioral results from the AI and mild impairment on standardized measures of recall are compatible with the hypothesis that, under some conditions, the retrieval of autobiographical event knowledge is qualitatively different from other forms of episodic retrieval (Chen et al., 2017; McDermott et al., 2009; Roediger and McDermott, 2013) (Figures 4, 5 and 6; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies and draws an inference about the nature of autobiographical memory.

claim: Remember-know responses and memory judgements on personally familiar stimuli can each be associated with activity in brain regions implicated in autobiographical recall.
source: Nonetheless, other studies indicate that remember-know responses and memory judgements on personally familiar stimuli, such as landmarks, can each be associated with activity in brain regions implicated in autobiographical recall (Elman et al., 2013; Frithsen and Miller, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the neural correlates of different types of memory judgments.

claim: Changes in retrieval orientation that emphasize either contextual or conceptual features of an autobiographical memory can modulate the distributed network of brain regions that support autobiographical retrieval.
source: Indeed, even changes in retrieval orientation that emphasize either contextual or conceptual features of an autobiographical memory can modulate the distributed network of brain regions that support autobiographical retrieval (Gurguryan and Sheldon, 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the effects of retrieval orientation on brain networks.
